title: 09 — System Design (LLD / Machine Coding)
html:
09 — System Design (LLD / Machine Coding)

HLD asks "what are the boxes?". LLD asks "what are the classes, what are their responsibilities, and what stops this from becoming a mess in six months?" LLD/machine-coding rounds test: requirement decomposition, OO modelling, correct use of patterns, extensibility, thread-safety, and whether your code compiles and runs.

1. The LLD method

flowchart TD
    A["1. Clarify requirements<br/>list functional + explicitly out of scope"] --> B["2. Identify entities<br/>nouns → classes; verbs → methods"]
    B --> C["3. Define responsibilities<br/>one reason to change each"]
    C --> D["4. Find the variation axes<br/>what will change? → interface there"]
    D --> E["5. Sketch the class diagram<br/>relationships + cardinality"]
    E --> F["6. Define the public API<br/>the 5-8 methods a client calls"]
    F --> G["7. Walk one end-to-end scenario<br/>sequence diagram"]
    G --> H["8. Code the core, mention<br/>concurrency + edge cases + tests"]

Time budget in a 45–60 min round: 5 min requirements, 5 min model, 5 min interfaces, 25 min code, 10 min extensions/concurrency/tests. Write compiling code, not pseudo-code. In-memory storage behind an interface is fine and expected.

The four questions that shape every LLD answer:

  1. What varies? → put an interface there (Strategy).
  2. What must never be invalid? → enforce it in a constructor or aggregate method.
  3. Who owns this state? → exactly one class.
  4. Is this called concurrently? → say so and handle it, even if only with a lock.

Relationship vocabulary (get this right in the diagram):

Relationship Meaning Lifetime Example
Association Knows about Independent Order ↔ Customer
Aggregation (◇) Has-a, shared Independent Team ◇ Player
Composition (◆) Owns, exclusive Dies with parent Order ◆ OrderLine
Inheritance (△) Is-a — CardPayment △ Payment
Dependency (- ->) Uses transiently — Service uses a DTO

2. Worked problem: Parking Lot

Requirements: multi-floor lot; vehicle types (motorcycle, car, truck) mapping to spot sizes; park/unpark; ticket on entry, fee on exit; pricing varies (hourly, flat, day-rate); show available spots per floor; multiple entry/exit gates (concurrent).

classDiagram
    class ParkingLot {
        -List~Floor~ floors
        -ISpotAllocator allocator
        -IFeeStrategy feeStrategy
        +Ticket Park(Vehicle v)
        +Receipt Unpark(TicketId id)
        +IReadOnlyDictionary~SpotSize,int~ Availability()
    }
    class Floor {
        -int Number
        -List~Spot~ spots
        +Spot? FindFree(SpotSize size)
    }
    class Spot {
        +SpotId Id
        +SpotSize Size
        +bool IsFree
        +Occupy(Vehicle v)
        +Release()
    }
    class Vehicle {
        +string Registration
        +VehicleType Type
    }
    class Ticket {
        +TicketId Id
        +SpotId SpotId
        +string Registration
        +DateTimeOffset EntryAt
    }
    class ISpotAllocator {
        <<interface>>
        +Spot? Allocate(IReadOnlyList~Floor~ floors, SpotSize size)
    }
    class IFeeStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +Money Calculate(Ticket t, DateTimeOffset exitAt, SpotSize size)
    }
    ParkingLot "1" *-- "many" Floor
    Floor "1" *-- "many" Spot
    ParkingLot ..> ISpotAllocator
    ParkingLot ..> IFeeStrategy
    Spot "0..1" --> "0..1" Vehicle

The variation axes (this is the design insight): how a spot is chosen (nearest-to-entrance, lowest floor, best-fit) and how the fee is computed (hourly, flat, weekend rate, EV surcharge). Both become strategies. Everything else is stable.

public enum VehicleType { Motorcycle, Car, Truck }
public enum SpotSize    { Small, Medium, Large }

public sealed record Vehicle(string Registration, VehicleType Type)
{
    public SpotSize RequiredSize => Type switch
    {
        VehicleType.Motorcycle => SpotSize.Small,
        VehicleType.Car        => SpotSize.Medium,
        VehicleType.Truck      => SpotSize.Large,
        _ => throw new NotSupportedException($"Unknown vehicle type {Type}.")
    };
}

public sealed class Spot
{
    private Vehicle? _occupant;
    public SpotId Id { get; }
    public SpotSize Size { get; }
    public int FloorNumber { get; }
    public bool IsFree => _occupant is null;

    public Spot(SpotId id, SpotSize size, int floorNumber)
        => (Id, Size, FloorNumber) = (id, size, floorNumber);

    internal void Occupy(Vehicle v)
    {
        if (!IsFree) throw new InvalidOperationException($"Spot {Id} is already occupied.");
        if (v.RequiredSize > Size) throw new InvalidOperationException(
            $"Vehicle {v.Registration} requires {v.RequiredSize}; spot {Id} is {Size}.");
        _occupant = v;
    }

    internal void Release()
    {
        if (IsFree) throw new InvalidOperationException($"Spot {Id} is not occupied.");
        _occupant = null;
    }
}

public interface ISpotAllocator { Spot? Allocate(IEnumerable<Spot> candidates); }

/// Fills the lowest floors first; among equals, the lowest spot number.
public sealed class LowestFloorFirstAllocator : ISpotAllocator
{
    public Spot? Allocate(IEnumerable<Spot> candidates) =>
        candidates.Where(s => s.IsFree)
                  .OrderBy(s => s.FloorNumber).ThenBy(s => s.Id.Value)
                  .FirstOrDefault();
}

public interface IFeeStrategy { Money Calculate(Ticket ticket, DateTimeOffset exitAt, SpotSize size); }

public sealed class HourlyFeeStrategy(IReadOnlyDictionary<SpotSize, decimal> ratePerHour) : IFeeStrategy
{
    public Money Calculate(Ticket t, DateTimeOffset exitAt, SpotSize size)
    {
        var hours = Math.Max(1, (int)Math.Ceiling((exitAt - t.EntryAt).TotalHours));  // part-hour rounds up
        return new Money(hours * ratePerHour[size], Currency.Gbp);
    }
}

public sealed class ParkingLot
{
    private readonly List<Spot> _spots;
    private readonly Dictionary<TicketId, Ticket> _active = [];
    private readonly ISpotAllocator _allocator;
    private readonly IFeeStrategy _fees;
    private readonly TimeProvider _clock;
    private readonly Lock _gate = new();          // .NET 9 Lock; use `object` on earlier versions

    public ParkingLot(IEnumerable<Spot> spots, ISpotAllocator allocator,
                      IFeeStrategy fees, TimeProvider clock)
    {
        _spots = [.. spots];
        _allocator = allocator;
        _fees = fees;
        _clock = clock;
    }

    /// Thread-safe: multiple entry gates call this concurrently.
    public Ticket Park(Vehicle vehicle)
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            var candidates = _spots.Where(s => s.Size >= vehicle.RequiredSize);
            var spot = _allocator.Allocate(candidates)
                ?? throw new NoSpaceAvailableException(
                       $"No free {vehicle.RequiredSize} or larger spot for {vehicle.Registration}.");

            spot.Occupy(vehicle);
            var ticket = new Ticket(TicketId.New(), spot.Id, vehicle.Registration, _clock.GetUtcNow());
            _active[ticket.Id] = ticket;
            return ticket;
        }
    }

    public Receipt Unpark(TicketId ticketId)
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            if (!_active.Remove(ticketId, out var ticket))
                throw new TicketNotFoundException($"Ticket {ticketId} is not active.");

            var spot = _spots.Single(s => s.Id == ticket.SpotId);
            var exitAt = _clock.GetUtcNow();
            var fee = _fees.Calculate(ticket, exitAt, spot.Size);
            spot.Release();
            return new Receipt(ticket.Id, ticket.EntryAt, exitAt, fee);
        }
    }

    public IReadOnlyDictionary<SpotSize, int> Availability()
    {
        lock (_gate)
            return _spots.Where(s => s.IsFree)
                         .GroupBy(s => s.Size)
                         .ToDictionary(g => g.Key, g => g.Count());
    }
}

Points to raise unprompted:

  • Concurrency: a single lock is correct but serialises all gates. Scale-up path: per-floor locks, or an atomic counter of free spots per size with Interlocked + a lock-free free-list. Say the simple thing first, then name the upgrade.
  • TimeProvider injection makes fee calculation testable without Thread.Sleep.
  • Extensions they'll ask for: reservations (add a Reserved spot state and a TTL), EV charging spots (a spot feature set rather than a new size — avoids a combinatorial enum), lost-ticket flat fee, monthly passes (a different IFeeStrategy chosen by customer type), persistence (put _spots/_active behind repositories).
  • Edge cases: double-unpark, unpark with an unknown ticket, a vehicle larger than any spot, exit before entry (clock skew), lot full.

3. Worked problem: LRU Cache (thread-safe)

Single-threaded version is in file 03 §10.1. The LLD version adds concurrency and TTL.

public sealed class ConcurrentLruCache<TKey, TValue> where TKey : notnull
{
    private readonly int _capacity;
    private readonly Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<Entry>> _map;
    private readonly LinkedList<Entry> _order = new();      // head = most recently used
    private readonly Lock _gate = new();
    private readonly TimeProvider _clock;
    private readonly TimeSpan? _ttl;

    private sealed record Entry(TKey Key, TValue Value, DateTimeOffset ExpiresAt);

    public ConcurrentLruCache(int capacity, TimeProvider clock, TimeSpan? ttl = null)
    {
        if (capacity <= 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(capacity));
        _capacity = capacity; _clock = clock; _ttl = ttl;
        _map = new Dictionary<TKey, LinkedListNode<Entry>>(capacity);
    }

    public bool TryGet(TKey key, out TValue value)
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            value = default!;
            if (!_map.TryGetValue(key, out var node)) return false;

            if (node.Value.ExpiresAt <= _clock.GetUtcNow())    // lazy expiry on access
            {
                Evict(node);
                return false;
            }
            _order.Remove(node);
            _order.AddFirst(node);
            value = node.Value.Value;
            return true;
        }
    }

    public void Put(TKey key, TValue value)
    {
        lock (_gate)
        {
            var expiresAt = _ttl is { } t ? _clock.GetUtcNow() + t : DateTimeOffset.MaxValue;
            if (_map.TryGetValue(key, out var existing))
            {
                existing.Value = new Entry(key, value, expiresAt);
                _order.Remove(existing);
                _order.AddFirst(existing);
                return;
            }
            if (_map.Count >= _capacity) Evict(_order.Last!);
            _map[key] = _order.AddFirst(new Entry(key, value, expiresAt));
        }
    }

    private void Evict(LinkedListNode<Entry> node)
    {
        _order.Remove(node);
        _map.Remove(node.Value.Key);
    }
}

Discussion points: a single lock caps throughput — real caches (Caffeine, MemoryCache) use striped locks plus a read buffer that records accesses without mutating the list on every read (amortised reordering). Mention W-TinyLFU as the modern policy that beats LRU on hit rate. Lazy expiry avoids a background sweeper but lets dead entries occupy capacity — pair with a periodic scan if memory matters.

4. Worked problem: Rate Limiter (library-level)

public interface IRateLimiter
{
    /// Returns true if the request is permitted, and how long to wait otherwise.
    bool TryAcquire(string key, int permits, out TimeSpan retryAfter);
}

public sealed class TokenBucketRateLimiter : IRateLimiter
{
    private sealed class Bucket { public double Tokens; public long LastRefillTicks; }

    private readonly ConcurrentDictionary<string, Bucket> _buckets = new();
    private readonly double _refillPerSecond;
    private readonly double _capacity;
    private readonly TimeProvider _clock;

    public TokenBucketRateLimiter(double refillPerSecond, double capacity, TimeProvider clock)
    {
        _refillPerSecond = refillPerSecond; _capacity = capacity; _clock = clock;
    }

    public bool TryAcquire(string key, int permits, out TimeSpan retryAfter)
    {
        var bucket = _buckets.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new Bucket
        {
            Tokens = _capacity,
            LastRefillTicks = _clock.GetTimestamp()
        });

        lock (bucket)                                     // per-key lock: no global contention
        {
            var now = _clock.GetTimestamp();
            var elapsed = _clock.GetElapsedTime(bucket.LastRefillTicks, now).TotalSeconds;
            bucket.Tokens = Math.Min(_capacity, bucket.Tokens + elapsed * _refillPerSecond);
            bucket.LastRefillTicks = now;

            if (bucket.Tokens >= permits)
            {
                bucket.Tokens -= permits;
                retryAfter = TimeSpan.Zero;
                return true;
            }
            var deficit = permits - bucket.Tokens;
            retryAfter = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(deficit / _refillPerSecond);
            return false;
        }
    }
}

Points to raise: per-key locking instead of one global lock; unbounded dictionary growth is a memory leak — evict idle buckets (an LRU or a periodic sweep); the distributed version needs the Redis Lua script (file 08 §7) because check-then-decrement must be atomic across processes; algorithm choice (token bucket allows bursts, sliding window is stricter) is a product decision.

5. Worked problem: Splitwise (expense sharing)

Requirements: users, groups; add an expense paid by one and split equally / by exact amounts / by percentage / by shares; show per-user balances; simplify debts.

classDiagram
    class ExpenseService {
        +Expense AddExpense(AddExpenseCommand cmd)
        +IReadOnlyList~Balance~ BalancesFor(UserId u)
        +IReadOnlyList~Settlement~ Simplify(GroupId g)
    }
    class Expense {
        +ExpenseId Id
        +UserId PaidBy
        +Money Amount
        +IReadOnlyList~Share~ Shares
    }
    class ISplitStrategy {
        <<interface>>
        +IReadOnlyList~Share~ Split(Money total, IReadOnlyList~SplitInput~ inputs)
    }
    class BalanceSheet {
        -Dictionary~(UserId,UserId),Money~ ledger
        +void Apply(Expense e)
        +Money Between(UserId a, UserId b)
    }
    ExpenseService ..> ISplitStrategy
    ExpenseService --> BalanceSheet
    Expense "1" *-- "many" Share
    ISplitStrategy <|-- EqualSplit
    ISplitStrategy <|-- ExactSplit
    ISplitStrategy <|-- PercentSplit

public interface ISplitStrategy
{
    IReadOnlyList<Share> Split(Money total, IReadOnlyList<SplitInput> inputs);
}

public sealed class EqualSplit : ISplitStrategy
{
    public IReadOnlyList<Share> Split(Money total, IReadOnlyList<SplitInput> inputs)
    {
        if (inputs.Count == 0) throw new ArgumentException("At least one participant required.");

        // Work in minor units so rounding is exact and the sum ALWAYS equals the total.
        long minor = total.ToMinorUnits();
        long each = minor / inputs.Count;
        long remainder = minor % inputs.Count;      // distribute pennies deterministically

        return [.. inputs.Select((p, i) =>
            new Share(p.UserId, Money.FromMinorUnits(each + (i < remainder ? 1 : 0), total.Currency)))];
    }
}

⚠️ The rounding question is the point of this problem. £10 split three ways is 3.33 + 3.33 + 3.34, never 3.33 × 3. Work in integer minor units, distribute the remainder deterministically (first-N users, or rotate by expense ID for fairness over time), and assert that shares sum exactly to the total — make it an invariant, not a hope.

Balance representation: store net pairwise balances (ledger[(a,b)] = +x means a owes b). Adding an expense updates Shares.Count − 1 entries. Debt simplification = a min-cash-flow problem: compute each user's net position, then greedily match the largest creditor with the largest debtor using two heaps — O(n log n), not optimal in the minimum-transactions sense (that's NP-hard) but standard and good.

Extensions to mention: multi-currency (store the FX rate at the time of the expense, never re-convert historically), settlements as a special expense type, an immutable event log for audit, concurrent edits (optimistic concurrency with a version column).

6. Worked problem: Elevator system

Requirements: N elevators, M floors, external requests (floor + direction) and internal requests (target floor), a scheduling policy, doors, emergency stop.

Model:

  • Elevator: id, currentFloor, direction (Up/Down/Idle), doorState, SortedSet<int> of stops.
  • ElevatorController: receives requests, assigns to an elevator via ISchedulingStrategy.
  • ISchedulingStrategy: NearestCarStrategy, ScanStrategy (the classic elevator/LOOK algorithm), FixedSectorStrategy.
  • Each elevator runs a state machine: Idle → MovingUp/MovingDown → DoorOpening → DoorOpen → DoorClosing → Idle.
// The scoring heart of dispatch — this is what the interviewer is looking for
public sealed class NearestCarStrategy : ISchedulingStrategy
{
    public Elevator? Assign(IReadOnlyList<Elevator> cars, HallCall call) =>
        cars.Where(c => c.IsOperational)
            .OrderBy(c => Cost(c, call))
            .FirstOrDefault();

    private static int Cost(Elevator c, HallCall call)
    {
        int distance = Math.Abs(c.CurrentFloor - call.Floor);

        // Moving toward the call, same direction → best (it can pick up en route)
        if (c.Direction == Direction.Idle)            return distance;
        if (c.Direction == call.Direction && IsAhead(c, call)) return distance;

        // Moving away or opposite direction → must finish its run first
        return distance + c.PendingStops * 2 + 1000;   // heavy penalty keeps ordering intuitive
    }

    private static bool IsAhead(Elevator c, HallCall call) =>
        c.Direction == Direction.Up ? call.Floor >= c.CurrentFloor : call.Floor <= c.CurrentFloor;
}

Discussion points: the SCAN/LOOK algorithm (serve all stops in the current direction, then reverse) is why elevators don't oscillate; each elevator should be its own concurrent actor (a Channel<Command> consumer) so the controller never blocks; the state machine must reject illegal transitions (move while doors open); emergency/fire mode is a global override — model it as a mode, not as flags scattered through the logic.

7. Worked problem: Logger framework

Requirements: levels, multiple sinks (console/file/remote), formatting, async/non-blocking, thread-safe, configurable at runtime, no message loss on shutdown.

public interface ILogSink : IAsyncDisposable { ValueTask WriteAsync(LogEvent e, CancellationToken ct); }

public sealed class AsyncLogger : IAsyncDisposable
{
    private readonly Channel<LogEvent> _channel;
    private readonly Task _pump;
    private readonly IReadOnlyList<ILogSink> _sinks;
    private volatile LogLevel _minimumLevel;               // hot-reloadable

    public AsyncLogger(IEnumerable<ILogSink> sinks, LogLevel minimumLevel, int capacity = 10_000)
    {
        _sinks = [.. sinks];
        _minimumLevel = minimumLevel;
        // Bounded + DropOldest: logging must NEVER block or OOM the application.
        _channel = Channel.CreateBounded<LogEvent>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity)
        {
            FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest,
            SingleReader = true
        });
        _pump = Task.Run(PumpAsync);
    }

    public void Log(LogLevel level, string template, params object?[] args)
    {
        if (level < _minimumLevel) return;                 // cheapest possible early exit
        _channel.Writer.TryWrite(new LogEvent(level, template, args, DateTimeOffset.UtcNow,
                                              Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId));
    }

    private async Task PumpAsync()
    {
        await foreach (var e in _channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync())
            foreach (var sink in _sinks)
                try { await sink.WriteAsync(e, CancellationToken.None); }
                catch { /* a failing sink must never break the app or the other sinks */ }
    }

    public async ValueTask DisposeAsync()
    {
        _channel.Writer.Complete();
        await _pump;                                        // flush before exit
        foreach (var s in _sinks) await s.DisposeAsync();
    }
}

Design points to say out loud: the level check happens before formatting (string interpolation in a filtered-out log call is pure waste — this is why ILogger uses templates and IsEnabled); bounded channel with a drop policy because backpressure into application code is worse than losing debug logs; per-sink failure isolation; flush on shutdown or you lose the crash logs you most need; structured events (template + args), not pre-rendered strings, so sinks can emit JSON.

8. Worked problem: BookMyShow / ticket booking

The hard part is not the model — it's preventing double-booking.

sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant B as Booking service
    participant D as Database
    U->>B: POST /holds {showId, seats[]}
    B->>D: BEGIN<br/>SELECT seats WHERE id IN (...) FOR UPDATE<br/>verify all Available<br/>UPDATE → Held, holdExpiresAt = now+10min<br/>COMMIT
    B-->>U: 201 holdId, expires in 10:00
    U->>B: POST /bookings {holdId, payment}
    B->>D: verify hold valid & not expired → Booked
    B-->>U: confirmed
    Note over B,D: Background job releases expired holds

Concurrency options, with the trade-off:

Approach Mechanism Pros Cons
Pessimistic lock SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the seat rows Simple, correct Locks held during user think-time if done wrong (don't — hold only during the state change)
Optimistic concurrency UPDATE seats SET status='Held', version=version+1 WHERE id=@id AND version=@v and check rows affected No locks, scales Retries under contention
Unique constraint A bookings(show_id, seat_id) unique index; let the DB reject the loser Bulletproof, simple Error-driven flow
Distributed lock Redis SET key val NX PX 30000 Works across services ⚠️ Not safe without fencing tokens; clock/GC pauses can break it

Recommendation to state: a short DB transaction with row locks (or optimistic version + unique constraint) for the hold. Never rely on a Redis lock alone for money-relevant uniqueness — the database constraint is the only real guarantee. Redis is an optimisation to reduce contention, not the correctness mechanism.

Other points: hold TTL with a sweeper job (and always check expiry at booking time — don't trust the sweeper); idempotency key on the booking endpoint so a retried payment doesn't double-book; seat-map reads served from cache with a version stamp; for a high-demand release, a virtual waiting room (queue tokens) is the real answer to 100k people hitting "buy" at 10:00:00.

9. Worked problem: File storage service (Dropbox-lite)

Model: File (id, ownerId, name, currentVersionId), FileVersion (id, size, checksum, blobKey, createdAt), Chunk (hash, size), Permission (principal, resource, level).

Key techniques to mention:

  • Content-addressed chunking: split files into ~4 MB chunks, hash each (SHA-256), store by hash → automatic deduplication across users and delta sync (upload only changed chunks).
  • Metadata in a relational DB, bytes in object storage. Never put blobs in the DB.
  • Presigned URLs: the client uploads/downloads directly to/from object storage. The API never proxies bytes — this single decision determines whether the service scales.
  • Merkle tree per file so client and server can find differences in O(log n) comparisons.
  • Conflict resolution: last-writer-wins with a conflict copy (file (conflicted copy 2026-07-27).docx) is what real products do; state that true auto-merge is only possible for known formats.
  • Sharing: ACL per resource with inheritance; check permissions on the metadata service, then mint a short-lived presigned URL.

10. Cross-cutting LLD topics interviewers probe

10.1 Thread safety — say something, always

Level Technique
Simplest correct One lock around mutable state
Better throughput Per-entity/striped locks; ConcurrentDictionary
Read-heavy ReaderWriterLockSlim, or immutable snapshots swapped with Interlocked.Exchange
Counters Interlocked.Increment
Pipelines Channel<T> — a single consumer removes the need for locks entirely
Best Immutability — no shared mutable state, no problem

⚠️ Never lock on this, a string, or a Type — external code can lock the same object and deadlock you. Use a private readonly lock object (or System.Threading.Lock in .NET 9+).

10.2 Extensibility without over-engineering

Put an interface at the axis you can name a second implementation for today. IFeeStrategy — yes, there are already three pricing models. IParkingLotFactory — no.

10.3 Validation and errors

Validate at construction (invariants) and at the API boundary (input). Throw domain-specific exceptions (NoSpaceAvailableException), not Exception. For expected outcomes, return a Result (file 05 §5.4).

10.4 Testability

Inject TimeProvider (never DateTime.Now), Random (seedable), and I/O behind interfaces. If a class needs a clock, a GUID, and a database to test one calculation, the calculation is in the wrong place.

10.5 What to name things

Use the problem's own vocabulary. In the parking lot: Spot, Ticket, Gate, Floor — not Manager, Helper, Processor, Data. Any class name ending in Manager, Handler, Helper, Util, or Info is a signal that you haven't decided what it does.

How to practise: 60 minutes, in an IDE, code must compile and have a Main that demonstrates the flow. Then spend 15 minutes writing the three extensions you'd be asked for and check whether your design absorbs them without rewrites — that's the real score.

12. LLD checklist

  • Requirements restated; out-of-scope stated explicitly
  • Entities named in domain vocabulary; no Manager/Helper
  • One clear responsibility per class
  • Variation axes behind interfaces; no interface with only one conceivable implementation
  • Invariants enforced in constructors/methods, not by convention
  • Value objects for money, IDs, quantities (no primitive obsession)
  • Enums/state machine for lifecycle; illegal transitions rejected
  • Concurrency addressed explicitly (even if "single lock, here's the upgrade path")
  • TimeProvider/Random/IO injected — deterministic tests possible
  • Edge cases enumerated: empty, duplicate, expired, concurrent, out-of-range, rounding
  • Errors: specific exception types or Result; nothing swallowed
  • Extension points named: "if you asked me for X, I'd add Y here"
  • A Main/test that demonstrates the happy path and one failure path
